plan.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent on a Loss Bowl: Learning Rate and Batch Size
plan.description: OFFLINE FIXTURE, not generated by a model. A bowl drawn as a wireframe of tubes shows the error (loss) for every pair of two model settings, a slope w and an intercept b. A marker starts on the bowl and each step moves it downhill along a noisy update, leaving a path of up to 40 points. Change the learning rate and batch size to see steps crawl, zig-zag or leave the plot.
plan.reason: You asked to change the learning rate and batch size. In an experiment you can change both and watch the path, the arrows and the numbers respond together, one step at a time.
interactions: Learning rate: small values creep, middle values reach the bottom fast, larger ones zig-zag across the steep direction, and past a certain size the run grows outward and stops as 'diverged'.
Batch size: with 1 point per step the path jitters and wanders near the bottom; bigger batches smooth it; at 64 the noise is exactly zero, so the path is smooth and the same every time.
Show or hide the grey full-batch update arrow. Compare it with the orange noisy update arrow: both include the learning rate and share one disclosed drawing scale.
Drag the start marker to a new spot on the bowl before you run.
Take one step: moves the marker by a single update so you can study it.
Use the card's step and pause controls to let the run continue (up to 40 steps) or to stop it.
New run, keep old path: starts again from the start marker with your current settings. The previous path stays in grey (up to 40 points) so you can compare.
assumptions: Simplified simulation: an idealized loss bowl with simulated batch noise, not a model trained on real data.
The loss is an exact bowl (a quadratic) with one lowest point. It is steeper along the intercept than along the slope.

Batch noise is simulated, not drawn from actual data points. Each step adds a random error to the exact gradient. Its spread is scaled the way it would be when sampling that many of 64 points without replacement, so it shrinks as the batch grows and is exactly zero at 64.
The update is: new settings = old settings − learning rate × noisy gradient.

Orange arrow: the noisy update (minus learning rate times noisy gradient). Grey arrow: the full-batch update (minus learning rate times exact full-data gradient). One drawing scale, 2 units of length per 1.0 of update, with a scale bar; an update of exactly 0 has no arrow and shows as 0.
Readouts: step number (out of 40), passes through the data (steps × batch size ÷ 64), full-data loss, and distance from the lowest point.

A run stops after 40 steps, or earlier as off plot when a step leaves the plotted area (the true position stays in the readouts). It is called diverged only when the learning rate is above 1.0, the limit this loss allows. The current path keeps at most 40 points, and so does the saved grey path.
Reset brings back the default settings and start point, clears both paths, and replays the same random noise from the fixed seed.
limitations: There is no real data, so the scene does not show data points, a fitted line or a real batch loss. The earlier batch-loss readout has been removed, and the noise is simulated.
A noisy step does not always lower the full-data loss. With small batches, single steps can go uphill. The loss falls only on average.
A bowl with a single lowest point cannot show the local minima, saddle points or flat regions found in deep-learning loss surfaces.
With small batches, unlucky noise can make a run diverge at a slightly smaller learning rate than with the full batch, or settle later.
The learning rate stays fixed, with no momentum, schedules or optimizers like Adam, so only your two settings change what happens.
plan.learningGoal: See that the learning rate sets the step size (too small is slow, too large overshoots or diverges), and that the batch size sets how noisy each gradient estimate is: small batches give jittery paths that wander near the bottom, and the full batch gives a smooth one.

geometries.text: Scale bar: an update of 1.0 is this long

assumptions: Offline fixture, not generated by a model. Simplified simulation: an idealized loss bowl with simulated batch noise, not a model trained on real data.
Loss L = 0.5(0.5 w² + 2 b²), lowest at w=b=0, steeper along b. New = old − learning rate × noisy gradient. With the full batch, b zig-zags above learning rate 0.5 and grows every step above 1.0.
Noise per component = 1.2 × N(0,1) × sqrt((64−B)/(63B)): 1.2 at B=1, exactly 0 at B=64. A noisy step can raise the full-data loss; it falls only on average.

Orange arrow: noisy update (minus learning rate × noisy gradient). Grey: full-batch update (minus learning rate × exact gradient). One scale, 2 units of length per 1.0 of update (the scale bar), no minimum or maximum length. An update of 0 has no arrow; its label reads 0.

The grey rim is the plot edge (|w| ≤ 4, |b| ≤ 2). A step crossing it stops the run and is marked where it crosses; readouts keep true values. Diverged only if the learning rate is above 1.0, else Off plot.
Readouts: loss, distance, step (of 40), passes through the data (steps × batch size ÷ 64). One update per 8 host steps. Changing a parameter restarts the run (same noise) and keeps the grey path.
Dragging the start moves it along w only (b stays 1.3) and restarts the run. Reset replays the same noise; New run, keep old path draws new noise.
